info.title: Workgraph control API
info.description:
The API behind the Workgraph interface, and the contract a tool integrates against.

Two credentials reach it. An interactive Cloudflare Access session, which the interface uses; and a personal API token, which a tool uses (ADR-0025). They resolve to the SAME application user, so every row-level security policy decides identically — authentication provenance is not an input a policy has. A token can only ever be narrower than its owner, never wider.

Conventions, enforced by a test rather than described here in hope: every collection is enveloped under a named key, never a bare array; every timestamp is RFC 3339 in UTC; every error is {error, code} with code from a closed set; every write accepts an optional Idempotency-Key.

post.description: The human act. Records the approver from the authenticated session, never from the request, so the token the client collects is attributed to a named person. Session-only, enforced the same way minting is: approving a grant is minting a token one step removed. A grant can be approved once.

403.description: A token cannot manage tokens

post.description: RFC 8628. Called by a client that has no credential and cannot open a browser — which is why it needs none. Returns a device_code (the client's secret, shown once), a short user_code for a person to type, and the verification URI to send them to. Poll /v1/device/token until it stops answering authorization_pending. Requesting an action a token may never hold is refused here rather than after somebody has approved it.

get.summary: What a device grant is asking for
get.description: Shows the approval page what is being asked — which client, which actions — so a person approves a described grant rather than an opaque code. Session-only: a token cannot read this, for the same reason it cannot mint one. Answers 404 identically for an unknown, expired or already-used code, so a mistyped code teaches nobody which codes exist.

403.description: A token cannot manage tokens

post.summary: Exchange an approved device code for a token
post.description: RFC 8628. Answers 400 with authorization_pending until a person approves, which is the normal answer for most of the flow's life; then expired_token or invalid_grant, or 200 with the token. Single use: a grant that has produced a token answers invalid_grant. The token is minted in the approver's name with the scopes they saw, and lives eight hours — a person approving an agent session is not agreeing to ninety days.

post.description: Runs one bead. The rig is chosen from the repositories the bead's project holds: exactly one candidate is used, none refuses with `no_rig_for_project`, and several refuses asking for one to be named. A named `rig` must be one of the candidates -- it chooses between them rather than opting out of the check, because dispatching a project's bead into a rig that does not hold its code produces a run that reports success having found nothing.

The answer is one result per repository - attached, already_attached or taken - so a repository held by another project is reported and skipped rather than discarding the rest of the batch. A repository is never silently reassigned: moving one changes who can see its pull requests. Accepts owner/name or a GitHub URL.

get.summary: What the platform is doing: cells, agents, queue, graphs and open alerts
get.description: One document rather than six endpoints: the caller is a page that draws all of it at once, and six round trips would show a half-consistent picture assembled from six moments. Company management only - organisation_admin or executive, granted organisation-wide - because the answer is about the platform rather than about any one project, so there is no per-row rule that would express it. Includes the count of beads attributed to no project, which is the failure that stayed invisible longest.

403.description: Authenticated, but not company management

get.summary: What happened to one bead: its outcome, the agent's own words, and what it cost
get.description: The answer to "I dispatched that - did anything happen?". `outcome` is derived rather than stored: `done` when the run succeeded AND the bead is closed, `blocked` when the run exited zero and left the bead open, `failed` when the run failed, plus `queued`, `running` and `never_dispatched`. The distinction matters - a run can exit zero having reported that it could not do the work, and `done` alone would read as success. `comment` carries the newest comment on the bead, which is where an agent explains itself. `spend` is broken down by model, because "which model was used" is a question a total cannot answer, and carries `newest_record` because usage arrives on an hourly import - a run that finished minutes ago shows no spend yet, and a zero would read as free.

post.summary: A rig reports which repository its working tree holds
post.description: Execution-node path (ADR-0019), service credential only. Reported by the node rather than configured centrally because the node is where the truth is: a rig is a working tree and its git remote says what it is a checkout of. This is the join that lets a dispatch be routed to a rig that can do the work, or refused - dispatching a project's bead into a disposable sandbox produces a run that reports success without doing anything (wg-ugb). A rig with no repository reports none, which is a fact rather than an omission: the witness and the mayor are rigs with no working tree.

get.summary: The rigs a cell should have, one per repository its projects hold
get.description: Execution-node path (ADR-0019), service credential only. The playbook reads this and provisions what is missing with `gt rig add`, so a repository attached to a project gets a rig and work can be dispatched against it. Provisioning rather than polling: creating a rig clones a repository and seeds agent infrastructure, which is minutes and gigabytes, and belongs in a deploy rather than a fifteen-second dispatcher pass. The rig NAME is decided here rather than by the caller, because the node reports rigs by directory name and a rig named differently in two places is a rig dispatch cannot route to. `prefix` is stable per repository, not per set: a bead id is permanent, so a prefix that renumbers when another repository is attached would corrupt ids already issued.

403.description: Not a service credential

post.summary: Open the pull request for work an agent landed
post.description: Execution-node path (ADR-0019), service credential only. The node has pushed a branch and asks for the pull request; it is opened here because opening one needs the GitHub App key, and a node that could open pull requests itself would need that key on the node. The repository is NOT taken from the request -- it is looked up from the rig, so a node cannot ask for a pull request against a repository its rig does not hold. Idempotent: a branch that already has an open pull request returns that one with `reused: true`, because a re-dispatched bead pushes another commit to the same branch and must not open a second.

job.description: The work_queue job that produced the change.

400.description: A required field is missing, or head and base are the same branch

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: A repeat under the same key replays the recorded success rather than acting twice. This endpoint is also idempotent without one: the branch is the natural key, so a retry finds the pull request already open and returns it with `reused: true`.

put.summary: Set or clear the command that says whether a change to this repository works
put.description: An agent has no shell -- its tools are read, search and edit -- so it cannot build or test what it writes, and a pull request otherwise arrives having never been executed. This is the command run against the change after the agent's run; if it fails, the agent is given the output and runs once more.\n\nOpt-in per repository, and a privileged act rather than metadata: the command executes code FROM the repository (`npm test` runs whatever package.json says) as the cell user, after an agent has been able to edit that file. The node narrows it by running with no git credential helper, so nothing it starts can mint a token or push. An empty command clears it, and a repository with none configured is never checked.
